analysis.one_liner: Bars giant online platforms from favoring their own products and from blocking rivals.
analysis.headline: Six senators from both parties introduced the bill, but it has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since June 2026 with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it illegal for the largest online platforms — companies with roughly $175 billion or more in annual revenue and platforms used by at least a third of Americans — to rig the field for their own products. It would stop them from burying competitors in search results, blocking rival apps from key features, forcing developers to buy other services, using data about businesses on the platform to build competing products, or locking users into default settings. The FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, with penalties of up to 10 percent of a company's U.S. revenue and expedited court hearings.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses and app developers that sell through big platforms, smaller competitors like independent search engines or music and shopping services, and everyday users, who get more choice, fairer search results, and the ability to change defaults on their devices. Enforcers also gain new tools, including expedited antitrust trials with judgments targeted within a year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small businesses, app developers, and platform users

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a giant platform to preference its own products over those of other business users in a way that materially harms competition, or to treat its own lines of business more favorably in search and ranking.

It bans platforms from restricting business users from accessing platform features, from tying access to purchases of other platform services, and from using nonpublic data generated by business users to build competing products.

It requires platforms to let users change default settings that steer them to the platform's own products, and bans discriminatory enforcement of terms of service among similarly situated business users.

The FTC, the Attorney General, and any state attorney general can enforce the law in federal court, with civil penalties of 1 to 10 percent of the violator's U.S. revenue, temporary injunctions, and possible forfeiture of executive pay for repeat offenders.
Court cases against covered platforms get priority docketing, with a goal of final judgment within one year of filing.

analysis.who_pays: The handful of giant platform companies that qualify under the size and reach thresholds, through penalties, compliance costs, and lost profits from self-preferencing and data advantages. Critics warn some costs could be passed to users through degraded or bundled services, and that forced data sharing could create privacy and security risks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Giant tech platforms, with possible user spillover

drawbacks.text: The rules are hard to draw. Forcing interoperability and limiting a platform's control of its own features could create security, privacy, and content-moderation problems, which is why the bill carries detailed affirmative defenses for safety, privacy, and fraud prevention that skeptics say could still let judges second-guess platform decisions.

The $175 billion revenue threshold is aimed squarely at a small group of very large companies, so critics call it selective; defenders say that is the point, since only platforms used by a third or more of Americans are covered.

Even expedited antitrust cases mean years of litigation, enforcement depends on the FTC and Justice Department choosing to act, and penalties are paid to the Treasury rather than directly to injured users or businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For small businesses and ordinary users, the upside is real: fairer search rankings, access to platform features, portable data, and easier switching between services. The downside is mainly the risk of clumsy enforcement — courts deciding how platforms should rank results or share features can produce unintended consequences — but the bill's affirmative defenses for safety, privacy, and fraud show its authors tried to account for that. The central tradeoff is concentrated gains for consumers and small sellers against a small group of very large companies' control over their platforms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has not received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced S. 4746 with five cosponsors across both parties — Sens. Klobuchar, Durbin, Hawley, Whitehouse, and Booker — on June 10, 2026.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action — no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote — has been taken, and Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027.

The bill's definition of a covered platform — at least $175 billion in average annual gross revenue and a platform reaching at least 34 percent of Americans over 12 — is drafted so it would apply only to the largest tech companies.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the giant platform companies: as long as the bill sits untouched in committee, the self-preferencing and data practices it would ban remain legal, and no enforcement or penalties exist.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The giant platforms, while the bill waits in committee

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor of the platform nondiscrimination bill.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: Cosponsor; ranking member of the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after it was referred to the committee he helps lead.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill across party lines, giving it a six-sponsor bipartisan group.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's six original sponsors split evenly between the parties (three Republicans and three Democrats), a leftover of the coalition that backed the earlier version of this bill, which a Senate Judiciary Committee approved 16-6 in 2022 before it died without a Senate floor vote; no member has acted against this version yet because it has not reached a hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Giant online platforms (companies like Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta)
industries.note: The bill directly outlaws the core practices that generate these companies' advantages on their own marketplaces, app stores, search engines, and services: favoring their own products in rankings, using business users' data against them, tying access to their platforms to buying other services, and locking users into defaults. Penalties reach up to 10 percent of U.S. revenue.

industries.industry: Small businesses and app developers that sell through big platforms
industries.note: These sellers rely on the largest platforms to reach customers and currently compete on terms the platform operator sets. The bill gives them the same features, fair rankings, portability of their own data, and protection from discriminatory rules of service.

industries.industry: Smaller tech competitors (independent search, browsers, shopping, and subscription services)
industries.note: Rivals benefit directly from bans on user lock-in and on restrictions of interoperability, which make it easier for users to switch away from defaults and for rivals to interconnect with dominant platforms.

These markets are the arenas where self-preferencing and data advantages play out. Consumers could see lower prices and more options if competition increases; the platform operators lose profits from steering, and some spillover costs could reach users through bundled or degraded services.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress ends January 3, 2027, and the bill has had no committee action since June. Very few bills introduced this late in a two-year Congress reach the floor; even the nearly identical earlier version, which cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee 16-6 in 2022 with broad public support, never got a Senate floor vote. The realistic path is the bill dying in committee at the end of this Congress unless the committee schedules a markup or the floor calendar opens, with the option of reintroduction in the next Congress.
